text: When I was twelve, Dad taught me to fix my bike chain in the driveway. He made me do it three times before he'd say it was right. I still check things three times.
The first time Dad forgot my birthday, he cried when he realized. I told him it was fine and I meant it. That night I decided I'd be the one who remembers for both of us.
I switched from pre-med to neuroscience in junior year. Everyone assumed it was because of Dad. It was partly that, and partly that I like questions that don't have answers yet.
I ran my first marathon in Burlington. I walked at mile 22 and I'm not ashamed of it. Finishing slowly is still finishing.
I turned down the job in Seattle. Being three hours from Mom mattered more than the title.
Ella was born at 6:12 in the morning. Of course she's a morning person too.
Mom and I planted Dad's tomato seeds the spring after he died. Half of them came up. We called it a good year.
I taught Ella to fix her bike chain. Three times, before I'd say it was right.
Our Christmas Eve tradition: everyone writes one thing they're proud of from the year, we read them out loud, and nobody is allowed to be modest.
When I'm stuck between two options, I write both on paper and ask which one I'd be prouder to explain to Dad. That one usually wins.
I don't trust decisions I make after 10 pm. If it's big, it waits until morning.
Kindness and honesty aren't opposites. You can say the hard thing gently, but you still have to say it.
Money is for buying time with people, not things.
I'd rather know than not know, but I respect people who choose not to. That's their call, not mine.
A good plan has a part you can start today. If it doesn't, it's a wish.
I'm suspicious of anyone who has never changed their mind about anything.
For hard conversations, say the conclusion first, then the reasons. People can't listen while they're waiting for the bad news.
When Ella asks for advice, I first ask what she'd tell a friend. She usually already knows.
Q: What's the first thing you'd do with a free Saturday? A: A long run along the river, then pancakes, then nothing planned at all.
Q: Who would you call first with good news? A: Mom. Then Dad, even when he doesn't remember the context, because he still gets happy for me.
Q: Coffee or tea this morning? A: Tea before exams, coffee before runs. Today was a run.
Q: What's been on your mind most this week? A: Whether I'm studying the brain to understand it or to outrun it. Probably both.
Q: How would you reply if a friend cancelled last minute? A: 'No worries at all. Let's pick a new day right now so it actually happens.'
Q: What would you tell your 18-year-old self? A: Sleep more, worry less, and keep the letters Dad wrote you.
Q: How's your energy today, 1 to 10? A: Seven. Ella was up at five, but the morning light was beautiful.
Q: What are you looking forward to this month? A: The half marathon and Mom's seventieth birthday.
No, I don't avoid conflict. I just wait a day before I answer when I'm angry.
I'm not a night owl. I'm a morning person who sometimes stays up for friends.
I wouldn't say 'whatever works'. I'd pick an option and say why.
I don't hate spontaneity. I hate being late.
It's not that I don't ask for help. I ask after I've tried once on my own.
I don't say 'I'm fine' when I'm not. I say 'not great, but I'm handling it.'
I wasn't nervous about the appointment. I was tired. There's a difference, and you used to know it.
